title: Terraform module outputs and extension points — design notes
body:
Purpose and scope:
This note captures design decisions for Terraform modules used by Private deployments (VPC + on-prem) with a focus on two areas that cause the most operational pain: the outputs surface and explicit extension points. The aim is to make modules composable, upgrade-friendly, and predictable for operator teams and customers who pin module versions in their private deployments.

Goals / principles:
- Minimal, stable outputs: only expose values consumers actually need (ids, connection strings, kubeconfig blobs).
- Extension without fork: provide well-defined hooks/extra_* inputs so customers can inject resources, labels, annotations, and policies without patching module internals.
- Backwards-compatible changes by default: use semantic versioning and a documented deprecation cadence.
- Cloud-agnostic intent: same high-level variables/outputs across AWS/GCP/Azure modules; provider-specific details encapsulated behind clear outputs.
- Safe upgrades: provide migration recipes for state-only changes and clear automation for breaking changes.

Module breakdown (recommended):
- network (vpc): manages VPC, subnets, route tables, NAT or egress, IGW, firewall rules for on-prem bridging.
- identity (iam): creates roles/service-accounts, IAM policies, mappings for cluster auth.
- cluster (k8s-cluster): wrapper around EKS/GKE/AKS primitives (control plane, nodepools, autoscaling config).
- nodepools: optional, separate lifecycle for worker groups.
- storage: manages block/volume classes and PV defaults for on-prem/backends.

Naming and variable conventions:
- variable names should be prefixed by component, e.g. vpc_cidr_block, iam_svcacct_name, cluster_k8s_version.
- allow maps for extensibility: e.g. map(string) for tags/labels and map(any) for provider-specific knobs.
- avoid nested complex objects in public surface unless absolutely required; prefer maps with documented keys.
- explicit sensitive flags for secrets: kubeconfig, service account keys must be declared sensitive in outputs.

Outputs: what to include and why
- Always include: 
  - vpc_id (string) — canonical reference used by other modules and customers.
  - public_subnet_ids / private_subnet_ids (list(string)) — consumers use these directly for ENIs, NAT attachments.
  - cluster_endpoint (string) and cluster_ca (string base64) — minimal kube access outputs.
  - kubeconfig_secret_ref (string) or kubeconfig (sensitive string) — depending on deployment pattern.
  - iam_role_arn (string) / service_account_email (string) — for cross-module binding.
- Prefer computed primitive outputs over provider-specific constructs: e.g. expose subnet ids rather than route table ids unless needed.
- Output naming should be stable across clouds: cluster_endpoint vs endpoint_url, prefer consistent names and list provider-specific variants under additional outputs (e.g. gke_master_ip).
- Sensitive outputs must be avoided where possible; prefer returning a reference to a secret (Vault/Secrets Manager) rather than raw value.

Extension points and hooks (non-invasive customization)
- extra_tags / extra_labels: map(string) applied to all created resources where supported.
- extra_iam_policies: list(string) — ARNs or policy JSON fragments that will be attached to the main role. Document the attach order semantics.
- resource_overrides (map(string)) — a small set of override knobs per resource, e.g., {"node_group.0.instance_type" = "c6i.4xlarge"}. Implement as documented locals that safely accept/ignore unknown keys.
- controller_annotations / kubelet_annotations for customers to add annotations without changing module.
- bootstrap_userdata or node_taint_map for custom node bootstrap logic.
- pre_create_hooks and post_create_hooks (list of command strings or small modules) — used by automation when customers need side-effects (DNS registration, firewall sync). These are intentionally primitive and executed by a companion provisioner resource only when flagged.

Cross-cloud differences and mapping notes
- VPC vs VPC-native: GCP has VPC-native subnets and different resource naming. Keep vpc_id and subnet ids as the canonical join points.
- IAM: AWS uses role ARNs, GCP uses service accounts (email), Azure uses managed identities. The identity module should expose a canonical identity reference (identity_reference) plus provider-specific outputs (role_arn / sa_email / principal_id).
- Load balancers and ingress: expose lb_dns_name and lb_ip_addresses; on-prem modules should support MetalLB or external IP allocations and expose the same outputs.

Upgrade and migration strategy (practical steps)
- Versioning rules:
  - patch: bug fixes only, no API change.
  - minor: additive changes, new optional variables/outputs are allowed.
  - major: breaking changes, required customer action documented.
- Deprecation policy: remove output/variable after 2 major versions with a clear deprecation message in plan/apply logs and in CHANGELOG.
- Migration mechanics (example): moving from exposing raw kubeconfig to secret reference.
  1) v1.2: add new output kubeconfig_secret_ref while keeping kubeconfig for parity.
  2) v1.3 (minor): mark kubeconfig as deprecated in docs and output description.
  3) v2.0 (major): remove kubeconfig output; provide terraform state migration script that creates a new secret resource and moves state references: terraform state mv module.old.kubeconfig module.new.kubeconfig_secret_ref (example wrapper script in /scripts/).
- Stateful rename example (terraform state ops): provide a curated script per module that runs under CI after a dry-run approval. Never instruct customers to edit state manually without support.

Rollout plan for customer workspaces
- Canary per-customer workspace: publish module version on a canary channel and roll to 3–5 low-risk workspaces first.
- Blue/green for cluster components: create new nodepool and drain old nodes, verify workloads, then destroy old nodepool.
- Automated rollback: if providers/plan fails, we must have documented state restore steps (state backup, terraform workspace snapshot, provider-level cleanup).

Testing and CI for modules
- Unit: validate formatting, variable descriptions, linting (tflint).
- Integration: terratest harness per cloud that deploys smallest footprint, verifies outputs match expectations, and tears down.
- Canary runs in staging: upgrade our internal customer-like staging environments as a final gate.
- Gate checks: detect output removals in PR and require a major version bump and migration plan ticket.

Examples (stubs)
- Variable style examples to document in README: 
  variable "vpc_cidr" {
    description = "Primary CIDR for the VPC"
    type        = string
    default     = "10.0.0.0/16"
  }

- Output example: 
  output "vpc_id" {
    description = "The created VPC id - canonical reference for other modules"
    value       = aws_vpc.main.id
  }

Decision log / rationale:
- Expose IDs, not provider internals: keeps cross-cloud consumption easier.
- Prefer secret references over raw secrets in outputs — reduces accidental leaks.
- Hooks are explicit inputs rather than callbacks executed by remote code. Simpler to reason about and audit.

Open questions / TODOs:
- Standardize a small SDK in Go/Python to handle state-migrations safely for customers.
- Decide whether to support a generic resource_overrides map or require provider-specific module forks for complex overrides.
- Finalize the deprecation cadence and automated tooling for churn detection across customer workspaces.

Operational runbook snippets (for support engineers)
- Quick-check after module upgrade failure: 
  1) terraform plan in a cloned workspace (state-only),
  2) check provider quotas and API limits,
  3) inspect CI terratest logs for last-green,
  4) if output removed unexpectedly, rollback state to backup and open a critical migration ticket.

References and artifacts:
- PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/infra/pull/789
- Migration epic: https://linear.app/REDW/issue/PIPE-412-module-outputs
- Internal guideline: https://confluence.redwood.ai/x/Priv-terraform-module-guidelines

Notes to reviewers:
- Focus review on whether extension points cover typical customer requests (extra_iam_policies, annotations, node bootstrap).
- Check whether any existing outputs in current modules leak sensitive values and recommend replacing with secret references.
- Provide suggestions for additional small helper scripts we can ship under infra/scripts for safe state transitions.

(End of design notes)
